_readme: Client-side rate and concurrency limits per provider (W4-04). Held as data beside their sources rather than in code, so every limit's provenance is reviewable where the number lives. The file is bundled into @adaptic/utils at build time: changing a limit ships as a release of this package and a consumer bump, not as a runtime switch. Every entry states where its numbers came from: `published` means transcribed from that provider's documented ceiling with a source link, `conservative-default` means the ceiling is not yet known and the client is deliberately slower than it needs to be. A guessed high limit and a known high limit look identical in config and behave identically right up until the provider starts refusing requests, so they are never allowed to look the same here. `scope` states the unit the provider enforces its limits in: `model` keeps one independent guard per model, `provider` (the default) one guard for all of the provider's models; a `model` scope cites its source like any published number (`source` when the entry is published, `scope_source` otherwise). `requests_per_minute_basis` overrides `basis` for the per-minute number when a provider publishes one bound and not the other, so the unpublished number never borrows the published label. A provider whose scope is `model` may carry a `models` map of per-model overrides: each override replaces the provider's numbers for that one model only, states its own `basis`, and is held to the same provenance rules as a provider entry. It exists for a model whose role differs from its siblings' (the closed incumbent that absorbs a whole alias's traffic when every leg above it is out), not to loosen a provider wholesale. `requests_per_minute` is a REFILL RATE and not a bucket size. `max_burst` is the bucket size: the most requests the guard admits in one instant, which the refill rate does not determine. The two are separate because a single number bounds only the long-run average, and a bucket sized at its own refill period starts full - so the first instant of a cold process admits the whole period's allowance, which a provider enforcing its ceiling over a shorter window refuses however correct that average is. An entry that declares no `max_burst` keeps the per-minute allowance as its capacity, which is the behaviour the guard has always had; the field is therefore added without changing any entry that does not set it. It is deliberately UNSET for the providers above whose numbers were sized against measured starvation of the live decision path, because tightening their burst is a separate decision that needs its own measurement rather than a side effect of introducing the field - and refusing a call on that path lost decisions outright, so the conservative direction there is not the tight one. It is REQUIRED of any provider serving a decision route this package guards, enforced by the limits verifier, because such a route is admitted against a vendor whose ceiling is enforced per second and a route admitted without a declared capacity is admitted with its burst unbounded. `max_burst_basis` overrides `basis` for the capacity, on the same rule as `requests_per_minute_basis`: a capacity derived from the client's own refill rate is the client's choice even where the entry's other numbers were transcribed. A `source` is a link wherever the provider publishes the figure on a page a reader can open; where the provider publishes it only inside an authenticated console, the source instead names what was read, when, and that it cannot be re-checked from this repository, because a figure nobody here can re-open is still a transcription and must not be dressed as a link nor demoted to a guess. A provider that meters INPUT TOKENS per second declares a second, independent bound here: `input_tokens_per_second` is the pace tokens are replaced at and `max_input_token_burst` the most admissible in one instant, each with its own `_basis` on the same rules as every other number. The two are declared together or not at all - a refill with no capacity bounds only the average a per-second ceiling does not enforce, and a capacity with no refill admits one bucketful and then nothing - and an entry declaring neither is held by no token bound, which is every entry that has ever been in this file. The capacity is set at or above the largest request the provider itself accepts, because a capacity below that makes a provider-legal request permanently unservable by this client.

defaults._readme: Applied to any provider whose published ceiling is unknown. Chosen to be comfortably below the slowest plausible published limit: being slower than necessary costs latency, while being faster than permitted costs 429s that the fallback chain will read as provider ill-health and use to open a circuit breaker. The asymmetry is what makes the conservative side the correct default.
defaults.note: Raised 2026-09-15 after the 4-concurrent ceiling was measured starving the live equity decision path: the alias chain reported 'exhausted its fallback chain' with every leg skipped by this guard (deepinfra primary+secondary and the anthropic incumbent), 173 of 473 signal-coordination calls failed (36.6%), and decisions were lost outright. Corroborating evidence at the time: ZERO 429s observed on any provider, the engine's own global fan-out gate permits 100 concurrent with 17 active, and 877 signal-analysis calls had been admitted to that gate. Concurrency and RPM are raised TOGETHER because they bind in series - lifting max_concurrent alone would only move the bottleneck to the token bucket. STILL conservative-default, NOT published: no provider console was read for these numbers, so they remain a deliberate under-estimate of an unknown ceiling. Transcribe the real tier limits (W3-07) and set basis to published.

anthropic.note: The unit is per model: the scope_source states 'Rate limits are applied separately for each model; therefore you can use different models up to their respective limits simultaneously', measured as requests, input tokens and output tokens per minute for each model class, with no concurrency ceiling. Each model therefore gets its own guard, so traffic on one model class (an Opus incumbent serving background aliases) cannot refuse calls to another (the Haiku incumbent of the hot-path alias). The NUMBERS stay conservative-default: the organisation's usage tier sets the real ceilings and is read only from the Claude Console rate-limits page, which has not been transcribed. The lowest standard tier listed at the source allows 1,000 requests per minute per model; organisations with limited history can start on an evaluation tier below that, which is why these values are held well under it. Transcribe the tier's limits (W3-07) and set basis to published.

claude-haiku-4-5.note: Raised 2026-09-28 for the closed-incumbent role this model holds on llm.fast, llm.decide and llm.extract. Measured that day: when DeepInfra was capacity-limited ('Model busy, retry later', timeouts at the 30000 ms hot-path budget), both DeepInfra legs of llm.fast opened their breakers and ALL of the alias's traffic fell to this model, where the 12-permit guard could not absorb it. In the 12 minutes to 15:33Z the incumbent leg recorded 18 timeouts, 15 breaker-open and 11 guard refusals ('did not admit the call within 15000 ms'), and the chain exhausted 20-45 times per 5 minutes. Sizing: in-flight demand is arrival rate times leg duration (Little's law), and the leg duration that matters is the worst case the chain permits, 30 s. 12 permits at 30 s serve 24 calls/min; 48 permits serve 96 calls/min at 30 s and up to the 300/min rate bound at haiku's normal single-digit-second latency, which covers the diverted llm.fast load plus normal llm.decide/llm.extract volume on the same guard. requests_per_minute is raised with it (the two bind in series) to 300, which is 30% of the 1,000 requests per minute per model that the scope_source lists for the lowest standard tier, so it remains below any standard tier's ceiling; no Anthropic 429 was observed in the window. acquire_timeout_ms is cut from 15000 to 10000 so an admitted call keeps at least 20 s of its 30 s leg budget: a call admitted after a 15 s wait had half its budget left, timed out at the provider, and that timeout was charged to this route's breaker, which then refused every call for the cooldown. STILL conservative-default: the organisation's tier has not been transcribed from the Claude Console (W3-07). Other Anthropic models keep the provider numbers.

deepinfra.note: Transcribed 2026-09-23 from the source, which states 'Every account has a default limit of 200 concurrent requests per model', that two models queried simultaneously allow 400 in total (200 per model), and that 'The rate limit is on concurrent requests, not per-minute volume.' Concurrency is therefore the bound DeepInfra enforces, and it is enforced per MODEL, so each model gets its own guard at 200. One guard shared by the whole account enforced a ceiling DeepInfra does not impose, and because an alias's primary and secondary are both served from this account, it refused the secondary exactly when the primary's queue was full. DeepInfra publishes no per-minute ceiling, so requests_per_minute is the client's own pacing backstop (requests_per_minute_basis: conservative-default), keyed per model like the bound DeepInfra does enforce. Exceeding the ceiling returns HTTP 429, and a very busy model can return 429 below it. The ceiling belongs to the account and this guard to one process, so every process calling the same model through the same account shares the 200.

groq.note: Declared primary of the hot-path llm.fast alias but blocked on open item OI-01. Held tighter than the default because a hot-path caller cannot afford to queue: if the limit binds, failing fast into the chain beats waiting.

openrouter.note: Aggregator backstop, reached by explicit route only. Held tight because its own limits are a function of whichever upstream it selects, which the client cannot observe.

typesafe.source: Two reads, because the entry's numbers come from two places. THE PER-SECOND CEILINGS: the organisation's own limits as its vendor console states them, read 2026-11-03 and relayed by the operator: 80 requests/second and 100,000 input tokens/second. Not a link: the vendor's docs page carries no figure and the console is reachable only by an interactive login, so this figure cannot be re-checked from this repository. THE PER-REQUEST CONTEXT CEILING, which max_input_token_burst is set at: https://docs.typesafe.ai/models.md states "64k tokens per request; 32k tokens for state plus the longest question", and that page is readable without a login.
typesafe.note: Provider of the typed decision routes dm.hosted and dm.hosted.preview, both of which the route table admits, so these numbers bind every call either route makes. THE VENDOR'S CEILING IS NOW KNOWN AND CITED, AND NONE OF THE NUMBERS BELOW IS IT. The docs page still carries no figure - https://docs.typesafe.ai/models.md section 'Rate limits' states, in full, 'Rate limits are set per organization. Your organization's current limits are in the developer console.' and 'Limits are measured in tokens per second and requests per second. A request over either limit returns 429 Too Many Requests.' - the API returns no rate-limit response header to read one from, and the console that holds the organisation's own limits needs an interactive login, so `source` names what was read there rather than a link. An earlier revision of this entry cited '100K tokens per second and 40 requests per second' to that same docs page; neither string nor either figure is present at that source, so the citation was withdrawn, and that is recorded here so a stale copy of it read elsewhere cannot quietly re-introduce it. The UNIT is the fact that survives every revision: the vendor enforces per SECOND, on requests and on tokens independently, and refuses over either. PACING, deliberately under the ceiling: requests_per_minute 1920 is 32 requests/second, 40% of the vendor's 80, and it is the client's own choice - requests_per_minute_basis is therefore conservative-default and not published, because a number the vendor did not give must never borrow the label of one it did. max_burst 32 holds the bucket to one second of that refill. The two quantities are independent: a bucket sized at the per-minute allowance starts full, so a cold process would admit sixty seconds of pacing in its first instant, and a ceiling enforced per second refuses that however correct the minute's average is. max_burst_basis is conservative-default on the same ground as the rate - it is derived from the client's own refill, not from the vendor. max_concurrent 32 matches the capacity on purpose, and raising it from 8 is the one limb of this entry that ENLARGES what may be in flight. The two bounds apply in series - the rate token first, then the permit - and each waits only acquire_timeout_ms, so a permit count below the capacity makes the capacity unreachable rather than redundant: at 8 permits and the latency band measured on these routes (281 to 313 ms for a one-question text call, 468 to 515 ms for a read over one 1024x768 image) the ninth call of a burst waits about a full call for a permit, past the 250 ms timeout, and is refused. Set equal, the bucket is the binding bound and the gate is the backstop it was meant to be, binding only when calls run slow relative to the refill. WHY THE PREVIOUS NUMBERS COST SOMETHING: a bucket of 10 refuses the 11th call of any instant, and such a refusal is the client's own - the vendor is never contacted, so the decision is discarded and nothing is learned about the provider either. The lane that sized this entry recorded, from the engine's decision-admission counters over the seven days to 2026-11-03, a peak of 126 hosted calls per minute with 29 inside a single second against that bucket of 10, 372 admission faults, and $2.42 of hosted spend; those figures are second-hand here and were not re-measured in this change, and the mechanism does not rest on them - any burst above the capacity is refused by construction, and the spend figure says only that the guard was not holding back a cost. acquire_timeout_ms stays 250, far below the 15000 package default. The bound the limits verifier enforces is the serving route's budget_ms, which is 1500 on both hosted routes; 250 is this entry's own tighter choice, because the queue spends the same budget the call does and a typed step that has already waited a quarter of a second cannot still answer inside a sub-second deadline, so it is refused as an admission fault and its caller moves on. THE TOKEN CEILING IS A SECOND, INDEPENDENT BOUND AND IS NOT GUARDED HERE: this package counts no hosted tokens, so nothing refuses a request on token grounds and the vendor's 429 is the only thing that will. At this pacing it is also the TIGHTER of the two bounds, which the request numbers above do not show. One 1024x768 image is billed 2632 input tokens (measured; the count follows the canvas and not the file size), so 32 requests/second of single-image reads is 84,224 input tokens/second, 84% of the ceiling, and a two-image request crosses the ceiling at 19 requests/second while the request guard still admits 32. Text-only traffic is nowhere near it: a one-question call measured 318 input tokens, 10% of the ceiling at 32/second. At the routes' own max_state_tokens of 32000 the fourth maximum-size request inside a second crosses it, and the worst instant this entry permits is 32 x 32000 = 1,024,000 input tokens, ten times the ceiling; it was already crossable at 8 permits (256,000, 2.6 times), so this change does not create the gap, it widens it fourfold. THE TOKEN CEILING IS NOW GUARDED, by a second bucket on the same guard identity, debited BEFORE dispatch by the request's own estimated input size and refused on the same acquire_timeout_ms as the rate bound. The two bind in series: a call admitted on requests and refused on tokens is raised as a typed capacity refusal and is never sent, and a call that states no estimate is refused on that ground rather than admitted on an unknown - a provider that refuses over a token ceiling cannot be paced by a client that declines to count. THE ARITHMETIC, so a reader can check it: a token bucket holding C and refilled at R admits at most C + R over any one-second window. max_input_token_burst 64000 is C and input_tokens_per_second 16000 is R, so no second admits more than 80,000 estimated input tokens, 80% of the vendor's 100,000 tokens/second - the SAME 20% the request limb holds back, where max_burst 32 plus one second's refill of 32 is 64 of the vendor's 80. C is the one number here taken from the vendor rather than chosen: it is the 64k per-request context ceiling its docs page publishes, and it is set there because a capacity below the largest request the VENDOR would accept makes a vendor-legal request permanently unservable by this client, which is a defect and not a guard. A request estimated above C is still refused, immediately and with that as its stated reason, because no wait could admit it and the vendor's own per-request ceiling would refuse it too. R is the client's own choice and its basis is therefore conservative-default. WHAT IT COSTS AND WHAT IT BUYS: text traffic is never bound by it - a one-question call measured 318 input tokens, so R alone sustains about 50 text calls/second, above the 32 the request guard admits. Image traffic IS bound by it, which is the point: one 1024x768 image is billed 2632 input tokens (measured; the count follows the canvas and not the file size), so the request guard's 32/second of single-image reads is 84,224 input tokens/second, 84% of the ceiling, a two-image request crosses the ceiling at 19 requests/second while the request guard still admits 32, and at the routes' own max_state_tokens of 32000 the worst instant the request bound alone permits is 32 x 32000 = 1,024,000 input tokens, ten times the ceiling. That worst instant was already crossable at the previous 8 permits (256,000, 2.6 times), so the capacity change widened an existing gap fourfold rather than creating it, and this bucket closes it at both sizes. Sustained, R admits about 6 single-image reads/second and C admits 24 of them in one instant. THE ESTIMATE IS RECONCILED, NOT TRUSTED: the debit is this client's estimate of a quantity only the vendor measures, so every answered call compares the estimate against the input count the vendor reported and the drift is recorded. An estimator nobody checks is how a guard silently stops guarding, and a systematic under-estimate would leave this bucket holding a ceiling it had drifted below. ROLLBACK of the token bound alone: remove input_tokens_per_second, input_tokens_per_second_basis, max_input_token_burst and max_input_token_burst_basis, and the guard applies no token bound at all, as it does for every provider that declares none. ROLLBACK: requests_per_minute 600, max_burst 10, max_concurrent 8, basis conservative-default, source null, and remove requests_per_minute_basis. It ships as a release of this package and a consumer bump, not as a runtime switch.
